q-43310.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14237869/assets/cce0e775722bbaaa8eeeb60a7cd097e8ad59b7c83c838f072416112aed657e33.png)

The area of ​​the triangle $△ABC$ is $\frac{21}{4}{\text{ cm}}^{2}.$ Find $AC.$
q-43310.worked_solution:
The formula for the area of the triangle is 

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}bc\operatorname{sin}⁡A,
$$

where $∠A$ is between the sides of lengths $b$ and $c.$ 

Here

$$
\begin{aligned}c & =AB=3\text{ cm}, \\ b & =AC, \\ m∠A & ={30}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since 

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡{30}^{∘}=\frac{1}{2},
$$

we can calculate $b=AC,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot b\cdot c\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡A \\ \frac{21}{4} & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot b\cdot 3\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡{30}^{∘} \\ \frac{21}{4} & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot b\cdot 3\cdot (\frac{1}{2}) \\ \frac{21}{4} & =\frac{3b}{4} \\ 3b & =21 \\ b & =7\text{ cm}.\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that $AC=7\text{cm}.$

Question 1
?

The area of ​​the triangle △ABC is 214 cm2. Find AC.

a
9 cm
b
223 cm
c
7 cm
d
10 cm
e
252 cm
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The formula for the area of the triangle is A=12bcsin⁡A, where ∠A is between the sides of lengths b and c.

Here c=AB=3 cm,b=AC,m∠A=30∘.

Since sin⁡30∘=12, we can calculate b=AC, as follows: A=12⋅b⋅c⋅sin⁡A214=12⋅b⋅3⋅sin⁡30∘214=12⋅b⋅3⋅(12)214=3b43b=21b=7 cm.

We conclude that AC=7cm.

q-67785.name: Question 2
q-67785.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14237869/assets/27dc9ff8452d9a9aa95322492549ba0eabed5f68a7aa2e586ebe239143268bde.png)

Rounded to the nearest integer, what is the area of the quadrilateral $ABCD?$
q-67785.worked_solution:
The area of the quadrilateral $ABCD$ is the sum of the areas of the triangles $△ABD$ and $△BDC$ (see the illustration below).

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14237869/assets/da7cc00005fbeb686443e2075009fda7c68f6d379a8ddb924a7dfe5b60e6ab16.png)

 

First we find the area for $△ABD:$ 
 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{ABD} & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 10\cdot 8\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡{75}^{∘} \\  & =40\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡{75}^{∘} \\  & ≈38.637,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

Now we find the area for $△BCD:$ 
 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{BDC} & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 5\cdot 12\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡{67.2}^{∘} \\  & =30\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡{67.2}^{∘} \\  & ≈27.656,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

Finally, we add together the areas of our two triangles to determine the area of $ABCD:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{ABCD} & ={A}_{ABD}+{A}_{BDC} \\  & =38.637+27.656 \\  & =66.293\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, to the nearest integer, the area of the quadrilateral $ABCD$ is $66.$

q-67785.html:
Question 2
?

Rounded to the nearest integer, what is the area of the quadrilateral ABCD?

a
 93
b
 82
c
 87
d
 58
e
 66
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The area of the quadrilateral ABCD is the sum of the areas of the triangles △ABD and △BDC (see the illustration below).

First we find the area for △ABD: AABD=12⋅10⋅8⋅sin⁡75∘=40⋅sin⁡75∘≈38.637, rounded to 3 decimal places.

Now we find the area for △BCD: ABDC=12⋅5⋅12⋅sin⁡67.2∘=30⋅sin⁡67.2∘≈27.656, rounded to 3 decimal places.

Finally, we add together the areas of our two triangles to determine the area of ABCD: AABCD=AABD+ABDC=38.637+27.656=66.293

Consequently, to the nearest integer, the area of the quadrilateral ABCD is 66.

q-161105.name: Question 3
q-161105.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14237869/assets/0b460a07026e489fb7c63dad99c04c7e44540138632626dcd3ebcafb5c0a93d3.png)

The area of $ABCD$ is $52{\text{ in}}^{2}.$   What is the area of $△BCD$ rounded to the nearest integer?
q-161105.worked_solution:
Let's start by finding the area of $△ABD.$ We get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{△ABD} & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot AB\cdot AD\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡A \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 9\cdot 16\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡{66}^{∘} \\  & =72\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡{66}^{∘} \\  & =65.775… \\  & ≈66{\text{ in}}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to the nearest integer.

The difference of the areas of  $△ABD$ and the quadrilateral $ABCD$ gives the area of $△BCD.$ Therefore, 
 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{△BCD} & ={A}_{△ABD}-{A}_{ABCD} \\  & =66-52 \\  & =14\,{\text{ in}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-161105.html:
Question 3
?

The area of ABCD is 52 in2. What is the area of △BCD rounded to the nearest integer?

a
14 in2
b
12 in2
c
15 in2
d
10 in2
e
16 in2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let's start by finding the area of △ABD. We get

A△ABD=12⋅AB⋅AD⋅sin⁡A=12⋅9⋅16⋅sin⁡66∘=72⋅sin⁡66∘=65.775…≈66 in2, rounded to the nearest integer.

The difference of the areas of △ABD and the quadrilateral ABCD gives the area of △BCD. Therefore, A△BCD=A△ABD−AABCD=66−52=14 in2.
